newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Blair says bust could follow British boom.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Blair says bust could follow British boom.

text.p: British opposition Labour party leader Tony Blair on Monday challenged Prime Minister John Major's claim that Britain had the strongest economy in Europe and said the current economic expansion could end in tears.
In a speech to business people in London, Blair reeled off statistics to buttress his argument that Britain was not nearly productive enough to rank as the strongest economy in Europe.
"There are underlying weaknesses in the economy that need to be addressed now if we are to avoid another bust and build prosperity that lasts," he said.
The Conservative government had placed Britain's economy on a roller-coaster since it took power in 1979 and given the country its two worst recessions since 1929.

"This instability is not a natural phenomenon visited upon us by the Almighty. It has been caused, to be frank, by the least competent management of any western economy in the past two decades," Blair said.
Under a Labour government, there would be no "go-it-alone" dashes for growth or demand management that ignored the way in which Britain's economy was linked with other economies.
"To that extent the Keynesian post-war consensus is over," he said.

Labour wanted a labour market that was not rigid or over-regulated. Labour had also buried the politics of tax and spend because it recognised that Britain's problems could not be solved simply by ever-increasing public spending.

"From now on, the battle will be over the way public money is spent and how best to reform the tax, benefit and welfare system to meet the demands of the new economy; and to do so on the basis of fairness and opportunity for everyone, not just a few. That is why we are committed to keeping tax as low as possible for ordinary families," Blair said.
He said Labour had no interest in "pressing the rewind button" on the economic policy changes he had ushered in since he became leader in 1994.

One of Blair's first acts as leader was to scrap Clause 4 of Labour's old constitution, which committed it to large-scale nationalisation. He replaced it with a new commitment to a strong enterprise economy.

Blair said that where there was no over-riding reason for preferring the public provision of goods and services, the presumption should be that economic activity was best left to the private sector and market forces.

"There should be no dogmatic belief that the private sector should do everything or that the public sector should do everything. It is the public interest today that is important. As we have made clear in our manifesto, what counts is what works."
